analysis.one_liner: Bans cruise ships from dumping sewage and wastewater near shore and sets national treatment standards.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2008 and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred cruise ships from discharging sewage, graywater, bilge water, sludge, ash, or hazardous waste into U.S. waters unless the waste was treated to strict federal standards and released at least 12 miles from shore, away from protected areas. It required EPA to set effluent limits, the Coast Guard to run inspections and place independent observers on ships, and it funded enforcement through a per-passenger fee on cruise lines. Ships could not dump sludge, ash, or hazardous waste at all and had to off-load it on land.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, beachgoers, fishermen, and everyone who uses or values U.S. ocean and Great Lakes waters. A single cruise ship can generate roughly 140,000–210,000 gallons of sewage and about 1 million gallons of graywater per week; the bill would have kept most of that out of nearshore waters where people swim, fish, and shellfish. It also protected cruise ship crew, who could not be fired for reporting violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Beachgoers, coastal communities, and ocean ecosystems

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits cruise ships from discharging sewage, graywater, or bilge water within 12 nautical miles of shore or in protected areas unless the waste meets strict treatment standards [S2][S3].
Outright bans dumping sewage sludge, incinerator ash, and hazardous waste into U.S. waters and requires those wastes to be off-loaded at land-based facilities [S2][S3].

Requires EPA to set effluent limits based on the best available treatment technology, and requires the Coast Guard to run annual unannounced inspections, public discharge logbooks, and a program of trained independent observers aboard each ship [S2][S3].
Funds the whole program through a per-passenger fee collected from cruise lines, so taxpayers do not pay for enforcement [S2][S3].
Protects crew members from being fired for reporting discharge violations, with reinstatement and back pay through the Labor Department [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cruise industry, which would have borne treatment equipment costs, inspection and observer programs, per-passenger fees, and civil penalties up to $25,000 per day plus criminal liability for knowing violations. Some of those costs could have been passed to cruise ticket prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cruise lines, via fees and compliance costs

drawbacks.text: The bill carved out all Alaska cruise operations for 10 years after enactment, weakening protection in the waters where most large-ship dumping debates were concentrated [S2][S3].
Compliance costs for treatment systems, observers, and per-passenger fees would fall on cruise operators, and ticket prices could rise as a result [S3].

Discharges meeting the treatment standards would still be allowed beyond 12 miles from shore, including treated sewage containing residual chlorine up to 10 milligrams per liter, a level some water quality advocates would consider too permissive [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental gains — keeping sewage, graywater, and hazardous waste out of nearshore swimming, fishing, and shellfish areas — are large relative to the costs, which are compliance expenses for a highly profitable industry. The main design weaknesses are the 10-year Alaska carve-out and the ability to dump treated waste beyond 12 miles, which leave significant pollution pathways open. On balance the bill would have done more good than harm for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the Clean Cruise Ship Act of 2008 on April 17, 2008 [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action appears in the record [S5].
No senator joined as a cosponsor, and the bill never advanced out of committee before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cruise lines came out ahead: they avoided strict national discharge standards, unannounced inspections, onboard observers, and per-passenger fees. Beachgoers, coastal communities, and ocean ecosystems lost the protections the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cruise lines avoided new rules and fees

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or markup, leaving it without a path to the floor

against.name: Cruise industry
against.role: Major shipping and tourism industry subject to the bill's discharge bans, inspections, and per-passenger fees
against.what_they_did: No documented support for the bill appeared; the bill's findings note the industry's own science panel opposed nearshore dumping, but the industry historically resisted federal discharge mandates

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; it had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required expensive treatment upgrades, annual unannounced inspections, onboard independent observers, per-passenger fees, and penalties up to $25,000 per day. Those costs exist because ships currently discharge enormous waste volumes — up to 210,000 gallons of sewage and 1 million gallons of graywater weekly per ship — into the same waters people use.

Cleaner nearshore waters protect swimming beaches, shellfish beds, and coral reefs that beachgoers and fishing businesses depend on. The bill's findings cite the U.S. Commission on Ocean Policy that cruise waste can threaten human health and damage shellfish beds and coral reefs.

The bill mandated advanced onboard treatment systems and a NOAA pilot program, with industry partners contributing at least 20 percent of project costs, to commercialize monitoring and treatment technology.
